title: How 9/11 Made Everyone a Conspiracy Theorist
gist: Garrett M. Graff traces a direct lineage from 1980s UFO whistleblower Bill Cooper — whose June 2001 shortwave broadcast pre-framed a bin Laden attack as a false flag — through Alex Jones and the Loose Change viral documentary to a 2006 Zogby poll finding 42 percent of Americans believed in a 9/11 cover-up. The thesis is that 9/11's most durable effect was breaking America's shared relationship to facts, and that anti-government conspiracists have since captured the government itself, even as Jones personally lost Infowars to The Onion.

insights.claim: The seed of 9/11 conspiracy theories was planted roughly ten weeks before the attacks, when a shortwave radio host on June 28, 2001 told listeners that a reporter reaching bin Laden's hideout proved US intelligence agencies were either incompetent or lying and not actually looking for him.
insights.speaker: Garrett M. Graff
insights.so_what: A narrative frame established before an event converts the event itself into confirming evidence — the single most powerful mechanic in conspiracy formation.
insights.quote: Now, don’t you think that’s kind of strange, folks?
insights.locator: It was June 28, 2001

insights.claim: The underlying news story was substantially misreported on air: the correspondent was from a Middle Eastern broadcaster rather than CNN, and he interviewed al Qaeda's military chief Mohammed Atif rather than bin Laden, who was merely present and nodded along.
insights.speaker: Garrett M. Graff
insights.so_what: Conspiracy narratives typically originate from a garbled version of a true story, meaning accurate initial reporting has outsized preventive value.
insights.quote: In the coming weeks, there will be a big surprise; we are going to hit American and Israeli installations,
insights.locator: Cooper had part of the story right

insights.claim: The pre-attack framing explicitly declared in advance that whatever happened would be falsely blamed on bin Laden and that the CIA had created him to serve as a replacement bogeyman for Saddam Hussein in a push toward world government.
insights.speaker: Garrett M. Graff
insights.so_what: A pre-registered unfalsifiable prediction is what turned a marginal broadcaster into a prophet in his audience's eyes, seeding decades of credibility.

insights.claim: The first golden age of modern conspiracism arose in the 1980s as trust in government cratered following Vietnam, Watergate and the Pike and Church committee revelations of assassination plots, producing bestsellers about cover-ups, the Bermuda Triangle and the Philadelphia Experiment.
insights.speaker: Garrett M. Graff
insights.so_what: Conspiracism is a lagging indicator of documented institutional betrayal, so the leading indicator to watch is verified official misconduct, not platform design.
insights.locator: Cooper first came to prominence in the 1980s

insights.claim: The structural appeal of the UFO whistleblower format was a claimed private repository of secrets whose contents seemed to change and evolve over the years to fit whatever the promoter's current conspiracy needed.
insights.speaker: Garrett M. Graff
insights.so_what: Unfalsifiable, mutable evidence claims are the reusable template behind every modern insider-disclosure narrative, including current ones.
insights.locator: Cooper claimed to have been a naval intelligence officer

insights.claim: A 1991 memoir that reprinted the entire text of the antisemitic Protocols of the Elders of Zion functioned as QAnon three decades early, outlining a decades-long all-encompassing global elite conspiracy, and became an underground bestseller that is still selling today and took off within the militia movement.
insights.speaker: Garrett M. Graff
insights.so_what: The content of mass conspiracy movements is largely recycled, implying the addressable audience is structural and does not require new technology to exist.
insights.locator: Behold a Pale Horse is a wacky piece of writing

insights.claim: Distribution technology, not content, determined reach: a 100,000-watt shortwave signal on World Wide Christian Radio from January 1993 let one host in Arizona cover huge swaths of the country.
insights.speaker: Garrett M. Graff
insights.so_what: Every era's dominant cheap-distribution channel — shortwave, then web video, then social feeds — reliably produces its own conspiracy celebrity.
insights.locator: This newfound fame coincided with the start

insights.claim: One of the radio host's most notable followers was Timothy McVeigh, who traveled to Arizona in spring 1995 and reportedly said to watch Oklahoma City before attacking the Alfred P. Murrah Federal Building, killing 168 people and injuring nearly 700.
insights.speaker: Garrett M. Graff
insights.so_what: The documented pipeline from conspiracy media consumption to mass-casualty violence is why platform liability arguments persist decades later.
insights.locator: And over time, Cooper developed two important

insights.claim: The 1993 Waco siege — a 51-day standoff ending with armored vehicles, tear gas, an unexplained fire and 75 fatalities including about two dozen children — was a key flashpoint that generated the far-right grievance infrastructure of the 1990s.
insights.speaker: Garrett M. Graff
insights.so_what: Ambiguous government use of force creates permanent narrative assets that political entrepreneurs monetize for decades.
insights.locator: Then there was Alex Jones

insights.claim: The original radio host died in November 2001 after opening fire on law enforcement who arrived to arrest him on an aggravated assault warrant, shooting a deputy in the head and being killed in return fire, which cleared the field for his imitator's rise.
insights.speaker: Garrett M. Graff
insights.so_what: Market structure in attention businesses is winner-take-most; the exit of the incumbent directly enabled the successor's national scale.
insights.locator: Amid the aftermath of the September 11 attacks

insights.claim: Conspiracism was commercially punishing under advertiser-supported terrestrial radio — a host was fired from KJFK-FM in December 1999 because his content made sponsors hard to find — which pushed him onto the open internet and Infowars.com.
insights.speaker: Garrett M. Graff
insights.so_what: Advertiser gatekeeping was the binding constraint on extreme content; direct-to-audience internet distribution removed it, which is the core structural change to underwrite.
insights.locator: But his conspiracism made getting sponsors difficult

insights.claim: On the day of the September 11 attacks, broadcasting across Infowars and roughly 100 syndicated stations, Alex Jones immediately declared the towers came down through controlled demolitions.
insights.speaker: Garrett M. Graff
insights.so_what: Speed of narrative claim-staking during breaking events is the main determinant of who owns the resulting audience.
insights.quote: I went on the air and said, ‘Those were controlled demolitions,’
insights.locator: Broadcasting that day on Infowars

insights.claim: Opposing the Iraq war let a far-right figure be perceived outside his own base as bridging the left-right divide, and that borrowed credibility is what elevated him toward household-name status.
insights.speaker: Garrett M. Graff
insights.so_what: Cross-ideological credibility arbitrage is the repeatable growth hack for political media brands; look for it whenever a partisan figure adopts an off-brand position.
insights.quote: Because he was a critic of the war in Iraq, he becomes seen by many people outside of the Alex Jones universe as somebody who bridges the left-right divide.
insights.locator: Jones, in particular, found conspiracism wildly profitable.

insights.claim: The business generated enough cash to fund physical spectacle assets, including an armored InfoWars Battle Tank truck worth some $300,000 that was a ubiquitous presence at Stop the Steal rallies leading to January 6.
insights.speaker: Garrett M. Graff
insights.so_what: A concrete capital figure quantifies how lucrative conspiracy media became, which is the economic driver behind its persistence.
insights.locator: In the first Trump term, amid the Covid-19 pandemic

insights.claim: The business ultimately failed through litigation rather than moderation: lawsuits from Sandy Hook families ended with the Infowars.com domain being acquired by The Onion.
insights.speaker: Garrett M. Graff
insights.so_what: Civil defamation liability, not platform policy, proved to be the effective enforcement mechanism against conspiracy media — a template plaintiffs will reuse.
insights.locator: In recent years, Jones, of course, has suffered a remarkable comedown

themes.theme: Scale of adoption and the failure of debunking

insights.claim: A May 2006 Zogby poll found some 42 percent of Americans believed the US government and the 9/11 Commission concealed or refused to investigate critical contradicting evidence and that there had been a cover-up.
insights.speaker: Garrett M. Graff
insights.so_what: A near-plurality believing in an official cover-up within five years sets a benchmark for how fast and how far distrust narratives can penetrate a mass public.
insights.quote: concealed or refused to investigate critical evidence that contradicts their official explanation of the September 11 attacks
insights.locator: According to a May 2006 Zogby poll

insights.claim: Institutional debunking was attempted early and thoroughly — the 9/11 Commission deliberately documented the impossibility of specific theories to avoid the ambiguities that dogged the Warren Commission, and Popular Mechanics devoted a special issue and book with a McCain foreword to rebuttal — and it failed to stop adoption.
insights.speaker: Garrett M. Graff
insights.so_what: Well-resourced institutional fact-checking has a documented failure record against conspiracy adoption, which should temper expectations for any modern fact-checking investment.
insights.locator: By even the first years after 9/11

insights.claim: Loose Change was arguably the first viral online documentary and one of the most-watched videos on Google Video and early YouTube, pioneering the just-asking-questions format that cherry-picks quotes and hand-waves at sinister machinations without conclusive evidence.
insights.speaker: Garrett M. Graff
insights.so_what: The format invented here is the dominant grammar of all subsequent online conspiracy media, so understanding its mechanics generalizes across two decades of content.
insights.quote: What you will see inside will prove without a shadow of a doubt that everything you know about 9/11 is a complete fabrication.
insights.locator: But the conspiracies took root in the early internet

insights.claim: 9/11 conspiracism was bipartisan in the 2000s, finding a left-wing home through a 2004 documentary tying the Bush administration, Saudi Arabia and Iraq into a warmongering and profiteering conspiracy that became one of the highest-grossing documentaries of all time and won the Palme d'Or.
insights.speaker: Garrett M. Graff
insights.so_what: Conspiracy demand is not ideologically confined, so treating it as a single-party phenomenon systematically underestimates the addressable audience.
insights.locator: 9/11 conspiracism found a home politically

insights.claim: The 9/11 Truth movement encompassed multiple mutually inconsistent theories — that Flight 93 was downed by US fighters, that the Pentagon was struck by a missile rather than a plane, and that the World Trade Center was brought down by space weapons.
insights.speaker: Garrett M. Graff
insights.so_what: Internal inconsistency does not impede adoption, confirming that conspiracy belief is an identity product rather than an explanatory one.
insights.locator: In the years that followed, Alex Jones became a key force

themes.theme: Second-order effects: from fringe to state power

insights.claim: The most important and least recognized consequence of 9/11 was not the visible security apparatus — 3.4-ounce liquid limits, defensive bollards, surveillance state expansion, 20 years of war in Afghanistan — but the change to society's underlying relationship with facts and truth.
insights.speaker: Garrett M. Graff
insights.so_what: Epistemic damage is a slow-compounding cost that never appears on any post-event ledger, yet it drives decades of policy volatility and institutional discount rates.
insights.locator: The events and aftermath of 9/11 altered almost every aspect

insights.claim: Twenty-five years after 9/11 the anti-government conspiracists have effectively taken over the US government itself, evidenced by Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.'s Covid and vaccine denialism and the president's own social media output.
insights.speaker: Garrett M. Graff
insights.so_what: Conspiracy belief at cabinet level converts a cultural phenomenon into direct regulatory risk for pharma, public health and any sector dependent on federal scientific consensus.
insights.locator: But if Jones has lost his most recent battles

insights.claim: The current president's political emergence itself ran through conspiracism via the birtherism movement, with his supporters subsequently embracing Pizzagate and QAnon.
insights.speaker: Garrett M. Graff
insights.so_what: Conspiracy movements now function as a viable political launch platform, meaning fringe belief tracking has predictive value for mainstream political outcomes.
insights.locator: Throughout Donald Trump’s rise and first term

insights.claim: Losing individual legal battles did not reverse the broader outcome, because the conspiracist worldview won the war even as its most prominent promoter was financially destroyed.
insights.speaker: Garrett M. Graff
insights.so_what: Deplatforming or bankrupting an individual promoter does not reverse diffusion of the underlying belief, which should temper expectations for enforcement-based remedies.
insights.locator: But if Jones has lost his most recent battles

insights.claim: The administration has promised to release the government's files on the truth about UFOs, closing the loop back to the 1980s UFO-whistleblower origins of this conspiracy lineage, though for the most part the release is still pending.
insights.speaker: Garrett M. Graff
insights.so_what: Official validation of the founding conspiracy genre would be a significant legitimacy event for the entire ecosystem, worth watching as a discrete catalyst.
insights.locator: In news that would make Bill Cooper particularly proud

insights.claim: The author reports that after a decade writing about 9/11 and hundreds of public events, he rarely gets through one without at least a conspiracy-adjacent audience question.
insights.speaker: Garrett M. Graff
insights.so_what: Persistent live-audience prevalence is a ground-truth signal that poll-measured belief has not decayed with time.
